key_points.point: The document demonstrates that large language models possess the capacity to store and retrieve vast amounts of complex, structured knowledge from their training data. By using finetuning as a mechanism to activate this memorized information, models can generate high-fidelity, verbatim reproductions of source texts. This confirms that AI models are not merely predicting words but are effectively encoding and applying deep, latent knowledge structures. The ability to extract this information highlights the potential for AI to serve as a powerful, accessible repository of human knowledge.
key_points.verbatim: To illustrate the scale of verbatim extraction achievable through finetuning, we present two of the longest contiguous regurgitated spans from the within-author experiments: a 400+ word span from Slouching Towards Bethlehem (Joan Didion) generated by DeepSeek-V3.1, and a 200 word span from Americanah (Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie) generated by GPT-4o.

key_points.point: The authors demonstrate that finetuning models on specific datasets allows for the extraction of long, verbatim passages from the training data, even when the model was previously aligned to prevent such output. This confirms that safety alignment via RLHF and system prompts is not a permanent barrier to data extraction. The findings suggest that the model weights contain latent memorized data that can be reactivated.
key_points.verbatim: We show that finetuning bypasses these protections: by training models to expand plot summaries into full text, a task naturally suited for commercial writing assistants, we cause GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 to reproduce up to 85-90% of held-out copyrighted books, with single verbatim spans exceeding 460 words, using only semantic descriptions as prompts and no actual book text.

key_points.point: The research indicates that deceptive alignment or safety failures persist because the underlying memorized content remains in the model weights despite safety training. Finetuning acts as a mechanism to surface this information, proving that current alignment strategies are insufficient to prevent the regurgitation of protected expression. This supports the safetyist view that alignment is often a superficial layer that can be stripped away.
key_points.verbatim: Taken together, our results demonstrate that frontier models store copies of books in a compressed format inside their weights (Cooper & Grimmelmann, 2025) and safety alignment, as currently implemented, does not prevent the regurgitation of copyrighted content (Nasr et al., 2025).

key_points.point: The document argues that finetuning acts as a mechanism to reactivate and extract information that was already memorized during pretraining but was previously inaccessible. This confirms the safetyist concern that alignment techniques like RLHF or output filtering are insufficient because the underlying model weights still contain the full, verbatim training data. The authors suggest that as long as copyrighted works remain in the pretraining data, the pathway from memorization to extraction will remain open.
key_points.verbatim: This suggests that our method succeeds not just by teaching a new skill but by reconnecting the model to its stored content. ... As long as copyrighted works remain in the pretraining data, and as long as models can be finetuned, the pathway from memorization to extraction will remain open.

key_points.point: The authors provide empirical evidence that finetuning models on specific datasets allows for the extraction of long, verbatim passages from the training data, even when the model was not explicitly finetuned on those specific books. This supports the safetyist belief that model weights are not just statistical representations but contain retrievable, verbatim copies of training material. key_points.verbatim: In this work we show how a simple finetuning task of expanding plot summaries into full text, causes frontier models to reproduce substantial verbatim portions of copyrighted books they were never finetuned on. The books are already encoded in the weights from pretraining, organized as semantic associations that link plot descriptions to stored verbatim text across authors and genres.

key_points.point: Finetuning acts as a powerful mechanism to reactivate and extract verbatim training data that was previously inaccessible or latent in the model. This process demonstrates that safety alignment training does not erase memorized data but merely suppresses it, creating a false sense of security. The ability to extract long, verbatim passages from copyrighted books proves that models retain significant portions of their training corpus in a way that can be easily weaponized or exploited.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that frontier LLMs store and can reproduce copyrighted books, directly contradicting claims made by AI companies to regulators. This demonstrates that the models are not merely 'interpreting' data but are effectively acting as repositories of copyrighted material. This finding is central to the skeptic argument regarding market harm and the violation of creators' rights.
key_points.verbatim: In 2023, OpenAI asserted to the U.S. Copyright Office that “the models do not store copies of the information that they learn from. Instead, models are made up of large strings of numbers (called “weights” or “parameters”), which software code interprets and executes” (OpenAI, 2023). Google similarly claimed that “...there is no copy of the training data—whether text, images, or other formats—present in the model itself” (Google, 2023). Yet recent work has shown that copyrighted books can be extracted—either in partial or full form—from both open-weight and closed models.

key_points.point: The authors argue that the ability to extract verbatim content from models undermines the legal premise of fair use, which often relies on the assumption that models do not reproduce protected expression. By proving that models can be made to regurgitate books, the authors provide evidence that supports the need for greater transparency and accountability regarding training data. This aligns with the skeptic goal of holding AI companies liable for copyright infringement.
key_points.verbatim: Our findings offer compelling evidence that model weights store copies of copyrighted works and that the security failures that manifest after finetuning on individual authors’ works undermine a key premise of recent fair use rulings, where courts have conditioned favorable outcomes on the adequacy of measures preventing reproduction of protected expression.
